rows.stem:
Consider the following chemical equation :

\(\mathrm{p\,Al + q\,H_2O \longrightarrow r\,Al_2O_3 + s\,H_2}\)

To balance this chemical equation, the values of ‘p’, ‘q’, ‘r’ and ‘s’ must be respectively :
rows.solution:
Balance aluminium and oxygen together: \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) needs 2 Al and 3 O, so take 2 Al and 3 \(\mathrm{H_2O}\). The 6 H atoms of 3 \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) give 3 \(\mathrm{H_2}\):

\(\mathrm{2Al + 3H_2O \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 3H_2}\)

So p, q, r, s are 2, 3, 1, 3, which is option (C) 2, 3, 1, 3.

rows.stem: Which of the given option represents a family of salts ?
rows.solution:
Salts with the same negative (or positive) radical belong to one family. \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\), \(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{CaSO_4}\) are all sulphates, so they form the family of sulphate salts. Each other choice mixes radicals.

This is option (B) \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\), \(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}\), \(\mathrm{CaSO_4}\).

rows.stem: The most common method of extraction of metals from their oxide ores is :
rows.solution: Metals in the middle of the reactivity series (zinc, iron, lead and others) are usually extracted from their oxides by heating with carbon, which is cheap and plentiful. This is option (A) Reduction with carbon.

rows.stem: Given below are the structures of some hydrocarbons. Select the two structures which are related to each other from the given options :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the four hydrocarbons (i)-(iv) are printed only as full structural formulas; naming them would state the answer (which two are isomers), so they are not described. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
Structure (ii) is a straight chain of four carbon atoms with ten hydrogens (butane, \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\)). Structure (iii) is a three-carbon chain with a fourth carbon branching from the middle carbon, also \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\) (isobutane, 2-methylpropane).

They have the same molecular formula but different structures, so they are structural isomers. ((i) is \(\mathrm{C_4H_8}\) with a double bond, and (iv) contains chlorine.)

This is option (C) (ii) and (iii).

rows.stem: Choose the *incorrect* statement about the common reaction used in hydrogenation of vegetable oils.

options.label: B
options.text: It takes place in the presence of nickel or palladium catalyst.

options.label: C
options.text: The product contains only single bonds between carbon atoms.

options.label: D
options.text: It is an addition reaction which occurs in the presence of an acid catalyst.

rows.solution:
Hydrogenation of vegetable oils is the addition of hydrogen across the carbon-carbon double bonds, in the presence of a nickel or palladium catalyst, giving a product with single bonds. No acid catalyst is used.

The incorrect statement is option (D) It is an addition reaction which occurs in the presence of an acid catalyst.

rows.stem:
Match Column-I with Column-II and select the correct option from the choices provided.

| Column-I | Column-II |
|---|---|
| a. Site of fertilisation of egg with the sperm | (i) Vagina |
| b. Site of implantation of embryo | (ii) Uterus |
| c. Site of entry of sperm into the female reproductive tract | (iii) Oviduct |
| d. Site through which the waste materials generated by the developing embryo are removed | (iv) Placenta |
|  | (v) Cervix |
rows.solution:
Fertilisation takes place in the oviduct, the embryo is implanted in the uterus, sperms enter the female tract through the vagina, and the embryo's wastes are removed through the placenta.

So a-(iii), b-(ii), c-(i), d-(iv), which is option (D).

rows.subtopic: Human Brain and Protection of Nervous Tissue
rows.stem: The part of the brain which maintains the posture and balance of the body is :
rows.solution: The cerebellum, part of the hind-brain, maintains posture and balance and makes voluntary movements precise. This is option (C) Cerebellum.

rows.stem: The plant hormone present in greater concentration in the areas of rapidly dividing cells is :
rows.solution: Cytokinins promote cell division, so they are present in higher concentration where cells divide rapidly, such as in fruits and seeds. This is option (B) Cytokinins.

rows.stem: Select a pair of bisexual flowers from the following :
rows.solution:
A bisexual flower has both stamens and pistil. *Hibiscus* and mustard flowers are bisexual; papaya and watermelon have unisexual flowers.

This is option (B) *Hibiscus* and mustard.

rows.stem: The gastric glands present in the wall of the stomach release :
rows.solution:
The gastric glands release hydrochloric acid, the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin, and mucus that protects the stomach lining. (Trypsin comes from the pancreas and salivary amylase from the salivary glands.)

This is option (C) Mucus and Pepsin.

rows.stem: Absolute refractive index of water and glass is \(\frac{4}{3}\) and \(\frac{3}{2}\) respectively. If the speed of light in glass is \(2 \times 10^8\) m/s, the speed of light in water is :
rows.solution:
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = n_g \times v_g = \dfrac{3}{2} \times 2 \times 10^8 = 3 \times 10^8\) m/s.

Speed in water: \(v_w = \dfrac{c}{n_w} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{4/3} = \dfrac{9}{4} \times 10^8\) m/s.

The options print \(\dfrac{9}{4}\) m/s without the factor \(10^8\), so none of them is correct. The marking scheme awards the mark to every student.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem: When a beam of white light passes through a region of very fine dust particles, the colour of light that scatters the most in that region is :
rows.solution:
Very fine particles scatter light of shorter wavelength much more than light of longer wavelength. Blue has the shortest wavelength of the choices, so it is scattered the most.

This is option (C) blue.

rows.stem: A wire of length ‘*l*’ is gradually stretched so that its length increases to 3*l*. If its original resistance is R, then its new resistance will be :
rows.solution:
Stretching keeps the volume of the wire the same. If the length becomes \(3l\), the area of cross-section becomes \(\dfrac{A}{3}\).

\(R' = \rho\dfrac{3l}{A/3} = 9\rho\dfrac{l}{A} = 9R\), which is option (C) 9R.

rows.stem: Which one of the following statements is *not* true about a bar magnet ?

options.label: A
options.text: It sets itself in north-south direction when suspended freely.

options.label: B
options.text: It has attractive power for iron filings.

options.label: D
options.text: The direction of magnetic field lines inside a bar magnet is from its north pole to its south pole.

rows.solution:
Field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole outside the magnet, and inside the magnet they run from the south pole to the north pole, forming closed loops.

So the statement that is not true is option (D) The direction of magnetic field lines inside a bar magnet is from its north pole to its south pole.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Solenoid
rows.stem: The strength of magnetic field produced inside a long straight current carrying solenoid does *not* depend upon :

options.label: A
options.text: number of turns in the solenoid

options.label: B
options.text: direction of current flowing through the solenoid

options.label: C
options.text: material of the core filled inside the solenoid

options.label: D
options.text: radius of the coil of the solenoid

rows.solution:
Inside a long solenoid the field is uniform, and its strength depends on the number of turns, the current and the material of the core. It does not depend on the radius of the coil.

Reversing the current only reverses the direction of the field without changing its strength, so the choice about the direction of the current can also be argued. The marking scheme accepts the radius of the coil, which is option (D) radius of the coil of the solenoid.

rows.stem:
Other than the abiotic components, which of the given biotic components are *not* required to make an aquarium with small herbivorous fishes a self-sustaining system ?

(i) Aquatic plants and aquatic animals

(ii) Terrestrial plants and terrestrial animals

(iii) Decomposers as bacteria and fungi

(iv) Consumers as clown fishes and sea urchins
rows.solution:
The aquarium already has the herbivorous fishes as consumers. To be self-sustaining it needs aquatic plants as producers and decomposers to recycle nutrients. Terrestrial plants and animals cannot live in it, and the marine consumers clown fishes and sea urchins are not needed.

So (ii) and (iv) are not required, which is option (D) (ii) and (iv).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Hydrogen gas is not evolved when a metal reacts with nitric acid.

**Reason (R) :** Nitric acid is a strong reducing agent and reduces the hydrogen produced in the reaction to water.
rows.context: For Questions number 17 to 20, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Hydrogen is not given off when a metal reacts with nitric acid, so the Assertion is true. The reason is that nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent: it oxidises the hydrogen produced to water and is itself reduced to oxides of nitrogen. It is not a reducing agent, so the Reason is false.

The Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.subtopic: Human Brain and Protection of Nervous Tissue
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** In our actions of writing or talking, our nervous system communicates with the muscles.

**Reason (R) :** Cranial nerves and spinal nerves form the peripheral nervous system.
rows.context: For Questions number 17 to 20, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
In voluntary actions such as writing or talking, the nervous system sends messages to the muscles, so the Assertion is true. The cranial and spinal nerves do form the peripheral nervous system, so the Reason is true.

But the Reason only names the parts of the peripheral nervous system; it does not explain the communication with muscles. Both are true and the Reason is not the correct explanation, which is option (B).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet never intersect each other.

**Reason (R) :** Magnetic field produced by a bar magnet is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction.
rows.context: For Questions number 17 to 20, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Field lines never intersect, because at a point of intersection the field would have two directions (a compass needle would point two ways), which is impossible. The Assertion is true.

The magnetic field has both magnitude and direction, so the Reason is true. The marking scheme takes the Reason as not explaining the Assertion, since it does not state that the direction at a point is unique.

Both are true and the Reason is not the correct explanation, which is option (B).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Use of jute bags for shopping reduces pollution.

**Reason (R) :** Jute is biodegradable and its bag may be reused as and when needed.
rows.context: For Questions number 17 to 20, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Jute bags reduce pollution, so the Assertion is true. They do so because jute is biodegradable and the bags can be reused many times, so the Reason is true and explains the Assertion.

This is option (A).

rows.stem: List the possible sources of energy required in decomposition reactions. Illustrate any one with a suitable example.
rows.solution:
The energy for a decomposition reaction can be supplied as heat, light or electricity.

Example (light): silver bromide decomposes in sunlight into silver and bromine,

\(\mathrm{2AgBr(s) \xrightarrow{\text{sunlight}} 2Ag(s) + Br_2(g)}\).

(Equally, heating calcium carbonate gives calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, or electrolysis of water gives hydrogen and oxygen.)

rows.stem: What is observed when hydrated ferrous sulphate crystals are heated in a dry boiling tube ? Give balanced chemical equation(s) of the reactions(s) that occur(s).
rows.solution:
Water droplets collect on the cooler upper part of the tube, and the green crystals turn white as they lose their water of crystallisation. On stronger heating the white solid turns brown (iron(III) oxide) and a smell of burning sulphur is noticed.

\(\mathrm{FeSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} FeSO_4 + 7H_2O}\)

\(\mathrm{2FeSO_4(s) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} Fe_2O_3(s) + SO_2(g) + SO_3(g)}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
rows.stem:
(a) Write the formula of the ions which (i) acids, and (ii) bases generate in water solutions.

(b) Dry \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas does not change the colour of dry litmus paper. Why ?
rows.solution:
(a) (i) Acids give hydrogen ions, \(\mathrm{H^+}\) (present as hydronium ions, \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\)). (ii) Bases give hydroxide ions, \(\mathrm{OH^-}\).

(b) Dry HCl gas does not form hydrogen ions without water. Since there are no \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions, it shows no acidic behaviour and does not change the colour of dry litmus paper.

rows.stem: State the main function of veins in human circulatory system. Why do they not need thick walls ?
rows.solution:
Veins collect deoxygenated blood from the different organs and bring it back to the heart.

They do not need thick walls because the blood in them is no longer under high pressure. (Valves in the veins keep the blood flowing in one direction.)

rows.stem:
(a) Explain how the proteins control the ‘characteristics’ in an organism with the help of an example of ‘tallness’ trait in pea plant.

(b) Name the section of DNA that controls the ‘characteristics’ in an organism.
rows.solution:
(a) A gene carries the information for making a particular protein. Tallness in a pea plant depends on the amount of a plant growth hormone, and the hormone is made with the help of an enzyme, which is a protein. If the gene gives an efficient enzyme, more hormone is made and the plant is tall; if the enzyme is less efficient, less hormone is made and the plant is short.

(b) A gene.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.subtopic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
rows.stem: A student has difficulty in reading his textbooks but can read the blackboard clearly while sitting in the last row. Name the defect of vision the student is suffering from. List two reasons due to which this defect arises. Write the nature of the lenses required to correct this defect.
rows.solution:
The student can see distant objects clearly but not nearby ones, so the defect is hypermetropia (far-sightedness).

It arises because (i) the focal length of the eye lens is too long, or (ii) the eyeball has become too small.

It is corrected with a convex (converging) lens of suitable power.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem: Draw a ray diagram to show the path of a ray of light falling obliquely on one of the refracting faces of a triangular glass prism and mark the angle of deviation on it.
rows.solution:
Draw a triangular glass prism. Let a ray (the incident ray) fall obliquely on one refracting face. On entering the glass it bends towards the normal; at the second face it bends away from the normal as it leaves (the emergent ray). Produce the incident ray forward and the emergent ray backward with dotted lines until they meet. The angle between them is the angle of deviation; mark it.

Draw arrows on the rays to show their direction.

rows.stem: An electric kettle is rated 230 V; 1000 W. Calculate the resistance of its heating element when in operation.

(a) What is a reactivity series of elements ? How is it developed ? Arrange the following elements as they are arranged in the reactivity series :

Aluminum, Calcium, Copper, Lead

(b) Write balanced chemical equation to show the reaction of iron (III) oxide \((\mathrm{Fe_2O_3})\) with aluminium.
rows.solution:
(a) The reactivity series is a list of metals arranged in order of decreasing reactivity. It is developed from displacement reactions: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt.

In the series: Calcium, Aluminium, Lead, Copper (most reactive first).

(b) \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 2Al \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 2Fe}\) + heat.

rows.subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
rows.stem: Common salt is an important raw material for various chemicals of daily use. State in brief the method of preparation of (i) Sodium hydroxide, and (ii) Sodium hydrogen carbonate from common salt. Write balanced chemical equations of the reactions that occur.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: its equation for (ii), \(\mathrm{2NaCl + H_2O + CO_2 + NH_3 \rightarrow NaHCO_3 + NH_4Cl}\), is not balanced (two Na and two Cl on the left, one of each on the right); one NaCl is needed, as written below.]

(i) Sodium hydroxide: electricity is passed through brine (an aqueous solution of sodium chloride). It decomposes to form sodium hydroxide; chlorine gas is given off at the anode and hydrogen gas at the cathode. This is the chlor-alkali process.

\(\mathrm{2NaCl(aq) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + Cl_2(g) + H_2(g)}\)

(ii) Sodium hydrogen carbonate: carbon dioxide and ammonia are passed through cold brine. Sodium hydrogen carbonate separates out, and ammonium chloride is left in solution.

\(\mathrm{NaCl + H_2O + CO_2 + NH_3 \rightarrow NH_4Cl + NaHCO_3}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
rows.stem: Design an experimental set-up to demonstrate that “Alcohol and glucose contain hydrogen but are not categorised as acids”. Also give the reason to justify this fact.
rows.solution:
Set-up: fix two iron nails in a rubber cork and place the cork in a beaker. Connect the nails, through a switch and a bulb, to a 6 V battery. Pour a solution into the beaker so that the nails dip in it and switch on.

Do this in turn with dilute hydrochloric acid (or sulphuric acid), with a glucose solution and with an alcohol solution.

Observation: the bulb glows with the acid solutions but does not glow with glucose or alcohol.

Reason: acids form hydrogen ions in water, and these ions carry the current. Glucose and alcohol contain hydrogen but do not release \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions in solution, so they do not conduct and are not acids.

rows.stem:
On the basis of the characteristics of the processes given in the brackets in each case, differentiate between the following :

(a) Products of breakdown of pyruvate in aerobic and anaerobic respiration in human beings (product(s) of the processes)

(b) Respiration and photosynthesis in plants (gas released)

(c) Respiration in terrestrial animals and fishes (organs involved)
rows.solution:
(a) Breakdown of pyruvate: in aerobic respiration the products are carbon dioxide and water (with much energy); in anaerobic respiration in human muscle the product is lactic acid.

(b) Gas released: respiration releases carbon dioxide; photosynthesis releases oxygen.

(c) Organs involved: terrestrial animals breathe with lungs (or through the skin in some); fishes use gills.

rows.stem:
A pure pea plant having round (R), yellow (Y) seeds is crossed with another pure pea plant having wrinkled (r), green (y) seeds. Subsequently \(\mathrm{F_1}\) progeny is self-pollinated to obtain \(\mathrm{F_2}\) progeny.

(a) What do the seeds of \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation look like ?

(b) Give the possible combinations of traits in seeds of \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation. Also give their ratio.

(c) State the reason of obtaining seeds of new combination of traits in \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation.
rows.solution:
(a) The \(\mathrm{F_1}\) seeds are all round and yellow (round and yellow are dominant).

(b) The \(\mathrm{F_2}\) seeds are of four kinds: round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green \(= 9 : 3 : 3 : 1\).

(c) Round green and wrinkled yellow are new combinations. They appear because the traits for seed shape and seed colour are inherited independently of each other (independent assortment).

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem: What is a rainbow ? Draw a labelled diagram to show its formation.
rows.solution:
A rainbow is a natural spectrum of colours that appears in the sky after a rain shower, in the direction opposite to the sun.

Diagram: draw a ray of sunlight falling on a spherical raindrop. At entry it is refracted and dispersed into its colours; at the back of the drop it is reflected internally; on leaving the drop it is refracted again, and the colours emerge spread out towards the observer. Label the sunlight, the raindrop and the dispersed colours, and draw arrows on the rays: the marking scheme deducts half a mark if they are missing.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Current-carrying Conductor
rows.stem:
Consider a rectangular cardboard having two holes P and Q through which a current carrying circular loop has been inserted as shown in the diagram.

(a) Make this diagram on your answer sheet and draw three magnetic field lines, one each passing through the points 1 (near P), 2 (at the centre of the loop) and 3 (near Q).

(b) List two factors on which the intensity of the magnetic field produced at the centre of the loop depends.

(c) Name the rule you will apply to determine the direction of magnetic field produced due to a current carrying straight conductor.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - (a) asks the student to copy the printed drawing and add field lines: a horizontal rectangular cardboard, a circular loop passing vertically through holes P and Q, points 1, 2 and 3 marked on the line PQ (near P, at the centre, near Q), and the loop's two leads leaving below the board. The sense of the current is shown only by arrows on the leads and is withheld here because it decides the direction of every field line. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
(a) Copy the board and the loop. Near P the field lines are small concentric circles around the wire where it passes through P; near Q they are concentric circles around the wire at Q, going round in the opposite sense. At the centre of the loop (point 2) the field line is a straight line, perpendicular to the plane of the loop.

(b) The field at the centre of the loop increases with (i) the current in the loop and (ii) the number of turns of the loop. (It is smaller for a larger radius.)

(c) The right-hand thumb rule.

rows.stem:
(a) “In a food chain energy flow is unidirectional.” Give two reasons for the given statement.

(b) If 10,000 J energy is available at the producer level, how much energy will be available to the secondary consumers ? Give reason to justify your answer.
rows.solution:
(a) Any two:

1. The energy captured by the autotrophs does not go back to the sun, and the energy passed to the herbivores does not come back to the autotrophs.

2. As energy moves to each next trophic level, it is no longer available to the previous level.

3. Energy is lost at each level, so the energy available keeps decreasing along the chain.

(b) 100 J. Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level reaches the next (the 10% law): 10,000 J at the producers gives 1,000 J at the primary consumers and 100 J at the secondary consumers.

rows.stem:
(i) Consider the following metals :

K, Ca, Al, Cu, Ag, Fe

Select from the above metals, a metal which

I. does not react with oxygen even at high temperature.

II. reacts with oxygen at ordinary temperature and forms a protective oxide layer which prevents the metal from further oxidation.

III. catches fire when kept in the open.

IV. does not burn in oxygen but the hot metal is coated with a black coloured oxide layer.

(ii) What are amphoteric oxides ? With the help of balanced chemical equations show that aluminium oxide is an amphoteric oxide.

(iii) What are alkalis ? Give one example.
rows.solution:
(i) I. Ag (silver does not react with oxygen even at high temperature). II. Al (it forms a thin protective oxide layer). III. K (potassium catches fire if kept in the open, so it is stored under kerosene). IV. Cu (copper does not burn, but hot copper is coated with black copper(II) oxide).

(ii) Metal oxides that react with both acids and bases to produce salt and water are called amphoteric oxides. Aluminium oxide reacts with both:

\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 6HCl \rightarrow 2AlCl_3 + 3H_2O}\)

\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH \rightarrow 2NaAlO_2 + H_2O}\) (sodium aluminate)

(iii) Bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis. Example: sodium hydroxide, NaOH (or potassium hydroxide, KOH).

rows.stem:
(i) With the help of balanced chemical equations state the process of extracting (I) mercury from its ore called cinnabar, and (II) copper from its sulphide ore.

(ii) Silver and copper articles slowly lose their shiny surfaces when exposed to air. Name the compounds formed on (I) silver articles, and (II) copper articles in the form of coating.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: its roasting equation for copper is printed as \(\mathrm{2CuS + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Cu_2O + 2SO_2}\), which is not balanced (two Cu on the left, four on the right); the ore is copper(I) sulphide, \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\), as written below.]

(i) (I) Mercury from cinnabar (HgS): the ore is heated in air, which converts it to mercury(II) oxide, and the oxide is then reduced to mercury by further heating.

\(\mathrm{2HgS(s) + 3O_2(g) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2HgO(s) + 2SO_2(g)}\)

\(\mathrm{2HgO(s) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2Hg(l) + O_2(g)}\)

(II) Copper from its sulphide ore (\(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\)): heating in air converts part of it to copper(I) oxide, which then reacts with the remaining sulphide to give copper.

\(\mathrm{2Cu_2S + 3O_2(g) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2Cu_2O(s) + 2SO_2(g)}\)

\(\mathrm{2Cu_2O + Cu_2S \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 6Cu(s) + SO_2(g)}\)

(ii) (I) Silver articles become coated with black silver sulphide, \(\mathrm{Ag_2S}\). (II) Copper articles become coated with green basic copper carbonate, \(\mathrm{CuCO_3 \cdot Cu(OH)_2}\).

rows.stem:
(i) Identify the parts ‘X’ and ‘Y’ in the figure given below :

(ii) Name the yellowish coloured structures produced by the part labelled as ‘Y’.

(iii) Write the name of the process by which these are transferred to the part labelled as ‘X’.

(iv) Explain the process of seed formation in a flowering plant.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - (i) asks to identify parts 'X' and 'Y' on a printed longitudinal section of a flower (petal and sepal are also labelled); which structures X and Y point at exists only in the drawing and is withheld here because it is the answer, and (ii)-(iii) build on those labels. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(i) X is the stigma and Y is the anther.

(ii) The anther produces pollen grains.

(iii) The pollen grains reach the stigma by pollination.

(iv) After pollination a pollen tube grows out of the pollen grain and travels through the style to reach the ovary. The male germ cell fuses with the female germ cell in the ovule (fertilisation) to form a zygote. The zygote divides several times to form an embryo within the ovule. The ovule develops a tough coat and is gradually converted into a seed.

rows.stem:
(i) Name the type of asexual mode of reproduction shown in the given figure.

(ii) Identify the unicellular organism in the diagram.

(iii) List any two advantages of asexual reproduction over sexual reproduction.

(iv) Name and explain any one mode of asexual reproduction observed in *Hydra*.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - (i) and (ii) ask to name the mode of reproduction and the unicellular organism from a printed six-stage sequence, labelled (a) to (f), of a single elongated flagellated cell dividing; neither the process nor the organism is named anywhere in the text. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(i) Binary fission (the cell divides into two along its length).

(ii) *Leishmania*.

(iii) Any two: many offspring are produced in a short time; the organisms survive better in unfavourable conditions; the offspring are genetically similar to the parent; no gametes are needed (a single parent is enough).

(iv) Budding: in *Hydra*, a bud develops as an outgrowth because of repeated cell division at one specific site. The bud grows into a tiny individual, and when mature it detaches from the parent and becomes a new independent individual. (Regeneration in *Hydra* is also an acceptable answer.)

rows.stem:
(i) “In refraction of light through a rectangular glass slab, the emergent ray is always parallel to the direction of the incident ray.” Why ? Explain with the help of a ray diagram. What happens when a ray of light falls normally on one of the faces of a rectangular glass prism ? Draw diagram.

(ii) An object is placed at a distance of 30 cm from the optical centre of a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. Use Lens formula to determine the position of the image formed in this case.
rows.solution:
(i) At the first face of the slab the ray bends towards the normal, and at the opposite parallel face it bends away from the normal by the same amount. The two bendings are equal and opposite, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, only shifted sideways.

Diagram: draw a rectangular glass slab, an incident ray falling obliquely on the top face, the refracted ray inside the glass bending towards the normal, and the emergent ray leaving the bottom face parallel to the incident ray (shown dotted, produced forward). Mark the normals and the angles of incidence and refraction.

When a ray falls normally on a face (angle of incidence \(0^\circ\)), it goes through without bending. Draw a ray perpendicular to the face of a rectangular slab passing straight through and out of the opposite face. (The marking scheme also accepts a triangular prism with the ray entering normally.)

(ii) For a concave lens, \(u = -30\) cm and \(f = -20\) cm. By the lens formula,

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{5}{60} = -\dfrac{1}{12}\), so \(v = -12\) cm.

The image is 12 cm from the lens on the same side as the object (virtual, erect).

rows.stem:
(i) A student wishes to study the image formation by a concave mirror using candle flame as object. State the type of the image formed by the mirror and mention the change in the image formed, if any, that he observes when the candle flame is gradually moved away from the pole of the mirror. Draw a ray diagram to show the image formation when the object distance is nearly equal to the radius of curvature of the mirror.

(ii) A convex mirror used for rear-view on an automobile has a focal length of \(3{\cdot}0\) m. If a bus is located at \(6{\cdot}0\) m from this mirror, use mirror formula to find the position of the image of the bus as seen in the mirror.
rows.solution:
(i) With the candle beyond F the image is real and inverted; with the candle between P and F it is virtual and erect. Once the candle is beyond F, moving it further from the pole makes the real image smaller and brings it closer to F.

Ray diagram with the candle at C: a ray from the top of the candle parallel to the axis reflects through F; a ray through F reflects parallel to the axis. They meet below the axis at C, so the image is at C, real, inverted and the same size as the object.

(ii) For a convex mirror, \(f = +3{\cdot}0\) m and \(u = -6{\cdot}0\) m. By the mirror formula,

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(v = +2{\cdot}0\) m.

The image is 2 m behind the mirror (virtual and erect).

rows.stem: In which one of the four test tubes is the foam formed the minimum ?
rows.context:
‘A’ and ‘B’ are two salts used for washing purposes. Salt ‘A’ is used for bathing also. Four test tubes I, II, III and IV as mentioned below are taken.

I. Rain water + solution of salt ‘A’

II. Rain water + solution of salt ‘B’

III. Tubewell water + solution of salt ‘A’

IV. Tubewell water + solution of salt ‘B’

The test tubes are shaken one by one almost identically for the same time and the lengths of foam formed in each test tube is noted.
rows.solution: Salt A, used also for bathing, is soap; tubewell water is hard. Soap forms the least foam with hard water, so the minimum foam is in test tube III (tubewell water and the solution of salt A).

rows.stem: Differentiate between salt A and salt B.
rows.context:
‘A’ and ‘B’ are two salts used for washing purposes. Salt ‘A’ is used for bathing also. Four test tubes I, II, III and IV as mentioned below are taken.

I. Rain water + solution of salt ‘A’

II. Rain water + solution of salt ‘B’

III. Tubewell water + solution of salt ‘A’

IV. Tubewell water + solution of salt ‘B’

The test tubes are shaken one by one almost identically for the same time and the lengths of foam formed in each test tube is noted.
rows.solution: Any one difference: salt A (soap) is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid, while salt B (detergent) is the sodium salt of a sulphonic acid or an ammonium salt with chloride or bromide ions. Or: soap does not form lather well with hard water, while a detergent forms lather even with hard water.

rows.stem: What are esters ? What happens when an ester reacts with an alkali (say sodium hydroxide) ? Give chemical equation for the reaction.
rows.context:
‘A’ and ‘B’ are two salts used for washing purposes. Salt ‘A’ is used for bathing also. Four test tubes I, II, III and IV as mentioned below are taken.

I. Rain water + solution of salt ‘A’

II. Rain water + solution of salt ‘B’

III. Tubewell water + solution of salt ‘A’

IV. Tubewell water + solution of salt ‘B’

The test tubes are shaken one by one almost identically for the same time and the lengths of foam formed in each test tube is noted.
rows.solution:
Esters are sweet-smelling substances formed when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst. They are used in perfumes and as flavouring agents.

With an alkali such as sodium hydroxide, an ester is converted back to the alcohol and the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid (saponification):

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5 + NaOH \rightarrow C_2H_5OH + CH_3COONa}\)

rows.stem: What is the cause of hardness of water ? Sometimes it is observed that while bathing foam is formed with difficulty and an insoluble substance is formed. Name this substance and write the cause of its formation.
rows.context:
‘A’ and ‘B’ are two salts used for washing purposes. Salt ‘A’ is used for bathing also. Four test tubes I, II, III and IV as mentioned below are taken.

I. Rain water + solution of salt ‘A’

II. Rain water + solution of salt ‘B’

III. Tubewell water + solution of salt ‘A’

IV. Tubewell water + solution of salt ‘B’

The test tubes are shaken one by one almost identically for the same time and the lengths of foam formed in each test tube is noted.
rows.solution:
Hardness of water is caused by calcium and magnesium salts dissolved in it.

The insoluble substance is scum. It forms because soap reacts with the calcium and magnesium salts in hard water to give insoluble calcium and magnesium salts of the fatty acids.

rows.stem: Name the hormone secreted in the blood of the person in this situation.
rows.context: A person while climbing up a rocky hill comes into a panic state and fear. His body starts reacting in a “flight-or-flight” condition to adjust to the dangerous and stressful situation.
rows.solution: Adrenaline.

rows.stem: Name the source gland of the hormone secreted in this condition.
rows.context: A person while climbing up a rocky hill comes into a panic state and fear. His body starts reacting in a “flight-or-flight” condition to adjust to the dangerous and stressful situation.
rows.solution: The adrenal gland.

rows.stem: State any two responses in the body of the person as a result of the secretion of this hormone.
rows.context: A person while climbing up a rocky hill comes into a panic state and fear. His body starts reacting in a “flight-or-flight” condition to adjust to the dangerous and stressful situation.
rows.solution: Any two: the heart beats faster, sending more oxygen to the muscles; blood supply to the digestive system and the skin is reduced, and blood is diverted to the skeletal muscles; the breathing rate increases because of faster contractions of the diaphragm and rib muscles.

rows.stem: How does the action of the chemical signal in terms of hormones differ from the electrical impulses via nerve cells ?
rows.context: A person while climbing up a rocky hill comes into a panic state and fear. His body starts reacting in a “flight-or-flight” condition to adjust to the dangerous and stressful situation.
rows.solution: A hormone is a chemical signal that travels through the bloodstream and reaches target cells all over the body; its action is slower but longer lasting. An electrical impulse travels along nerve cells only to the cells they connect, and acts quickly.

rows.stem: Which one of the graphs represents the series combination of \(\mathrm{R_1}\) and \(\mathrm{R_2}\) ?
rows.context:
As shown in the diagram, an electric circuit consisting of an ammeter, a voltmeter, 4 cells of \(1{\cdot}5\) V each, a plug key with a gap XY was set up. Voltmeter and ammeter readings were recorded in the observation table for four arrangements as given below :

Arrangement No. 1 – only resistor \(\mathrm{R_1}\) in gap XY

Arrangement No. 2 – only resistor \(\mathrm{R_2}\) in gap XY

Arrangement No. 3 – Resistors \(\mathrm{R_1}\) and \(\mathrm{R_2}\) in series in gap XY

Arrangement No. 4 – Resistors \(\mathrm{R_1}\) and \(\mathrm{R_2}\) in parallel in gap XY

Based on the observations, four V – I graphs A, B, C and D as shown in figure were drawn. Study these graphs.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the answer is read off the printed V-I graph: four straight lines A, B, C and D from the origin O, I (amperes) on the vertical axis and V (volts) on the horizontal, with no tick values; their relative slopes are withheld here because they are the answer. (The circuit on page idx 24 is described fully in the passage.) Page idx 26.
rows.solution: In the V-I graph the slope \(\dfrac{I}{V} = \dfrac{1}{R}\). The series combination has the largest resistance, so its line has the smallest slope. That is graph A, the least steep line.

rows.stem: Show an arrangement of three resistors, each of resistance \(10\,\Omega\), so that the combination has a resistance of \(15\,\Omega\). Give justification for your answer.
rows.context:
As shown in the diagram, an electric circuit consisting of an ammeter, a voltmeter, 4 cells of \(1{\cdot}5\) V each, a plug key with a gap XY was set up. Voltmeter and ammeter readings were recorded in the observation table for four arrangements as given below :

Arrangement No. 1 – only resistor \(\mathrm{R_1}\) in gap XY

Arrangement No. 2 – only resistor \(\mathrm{R_2}\) in gap XY

Arrangement No. 3 – Resistors \(\mathrm{R_1}\) and \(\mathrm{R_2}\) in series in gap XY

Arrangement No. 4 – Resistors \(\mathrm{R_1}\) and \(\mathrm{R_2}\) in parallel in gap XY

Based on the observations, four V – I graphs A, B, C and D as shown in figure were drawn. Study these graphs.
rows.solution:
Connect two of the \(10\,\Omega\) resistors in parallel, and connect the third in series with this pair.

The parallel pair has resistance \(\dfrac{10 \times 10}{10 + 10} = 5\,\Omega\), and adding the third in series gives \(5 + 10 = 15\,\Omega\).

rows.stem: A battery of 6 V is connected with a series combination of five resistors of \(0{\cdot}1\,\Omega\), \(0{\cdot}2\,\Omega\), \(0{\cdot}3\,\Omega\), \(0{\cdot}4\,\Omega\) and \(0{\cdot}5\,\Omega\). How much current would flow through the \(0{\cdot}3\,\Omega\) resistor ? Justify your answer.
rows.context:
As shown in the diagram, an electric circuit consisting of an ammeter, a voltmeter, 4 cells of \(1{\cdot}5\) V each, a plug key with a gap XY was set up. Voltmeter and ammeter readings were recorded in the observation table for four arrangements as given below :

Arrangement No. 1 – only resistor \(\mathrm{R_1}\) in gap XY

Arrangement No. 2 – only resistor \(\mathrm{R_2}\) in gap XY

Arrangement No. 3 – Resistors \(\mathrm{R_1}\) and \(\mathrm{R_2}\) in series in gap XY

Arrangement No. 4 – Resistors \(\mathrm{R_1}\) and \(\mathrm{R_2}\) in parallel in gap XY

Based on the observations, four V – I graphs A, B, C and D as shown in figure were drawn. Study these graphs.
rows.solution:
Total resistance in series \(= 0{\cdot}1 + 0{\cdot}2 + 0{\cdot}3 + 0{\cdot}4 + 0{\cdot}5 = 1{\cdot}5\,\Omega\).

Current \(I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{6}{1{\cdot}5} = 4\) A.

The same current flows through every resistor in a series combination, so 4 A flows through the \(0{\cdot}3\,\Omega\) resistor.
